title: Map Skills: Scale, Direction and Topographic Maps
summary: The three types of scale, measuring and calculating distance, compass directions and bearings, map symbols, and showing height on topographic maps.

notes.text: **Scale** tells us how much smaller the map is than the real area. It shows the relationship between a distance on the map and the same distance on the ground.

notes.caption: Three ways of showing scale
rows: 1 unit on the map = 50 000 of the same units on the ground
A ruled line divided into kilometres
Measure on the map and compare with the line

notes.problem: Write the scale 1 : 50 000 as a word scale in kilometres.
steps: 1 cm on the map = 50 000 cm on the ground.

notes.title: Calculating real distance
notes.problem: On a 1 : 50 000 map, two farms are 6,4 cm apart. What is the real distance?

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: **Large-scale** maps (e.g. 1 : 10 000) show a small area in a lot of detail, like a town plan. **Small-scale** maps (e.g. 1 : 10 000 000) show a large area with little detail, like a map of Africa. To measure a curved road or river, lay a piece of string along it, then measure the string.
There are **16 compass directions**: the four cardinal points (N, E, S, W), the four intermediate points (NE, SE, SW, NW) and eight more (NNE, ENE, ESE, SSE, SSW, WSW, WNW, NNW).
The angle measured **clockwise from true north** to a line joining two points. Bearings are always written with three digits, from 000° to 360°, e.g. east = 090°.

Maps use **symbols**, colours and abbreviations to show features. These are explained in the **key** (legend). On South African topographic maps, for example: blue for water features, green for cultivated land and orchards, brown for contour lines, red or black for roads, and black for buildings and railways.

items: **Contour lines**: brown lines joining places of the same height above sea level. Lines close together show a **steep** slope; lines far apart show a **gentle** slope.
**Spot heights**: a dot with a number showing the exact height (e.g. • 1 425).
**Trigonometrical stations**: a triangle with a number, marking an accurately surveyed point, usually on a hilltop.
**Contour interval**: the vertical difference between two neighbouring contour lines, usually 20 m on 1 : 50 000 maps.
